title: OneLake: The Unified Data Lake at the Heart of Microsoft Fabric
summary: OneLake is the single, tenant-wide logical data lake that underpins every Microsoft Fabric experience. This article explains the architecture, shortcut system, security model, and internal mechanics that make OneLake the common storage fabric for T-SQL, Spark, Power BI, and every other Fabric engine.
body_md:
## What Is OneLake and Why Does It Matter?

Every Microsoft Fabric tenant is provisioned with exactly one OneLake — no more, no less [S2]. It is the single logical data lake for the entire organization, built on Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, and every Fabric compute experience comes preconfigured to use it as its native store [S1]. The design is deliberately analogous to how Office applications automatically save to the organization's OneDrive: storage is just there, unified, and ready [S1].

For practitioners used to managing separate data lakes per team or business unit, this represents a meaningful shift. Before OneLake, it was common to provision independent physical storage accounts for each group, which scattered governance, duplicated data, and forced painful integration work. That pattern is now unnecessary and actively counterproductive [S2].

All Fabric data items — lakehouses, warehouses, KQL databases, and others — automatically persist their tabular data as Delta-Parquet files in OneLake [S2]. There is no separate "upload to storage" step. The moment you create a lakehouse or warehouse, the data lives in OneLake.

![OneLake architecture, namespace, shortcuts, storage format, and security model](/content/diagrams/onelake-architecture.svg)

## Core Architecture: One Namespace, Every Engine

### A Single File-System Namespace

OneLake provides one file-system namespace that spans all users, regions, and workspaces within the tenant [S1]. Internally, the addressing model virtualizes the entire tenant as a single giant ADLS storage account: each Fabric workspace maps to a container, and each Fabric item within that workspace maps to a directory [S2]. This means that every path in OneLake is globally unambiguous within the tenant — a Spark notebook and a T-SQL query can reference the same physical file with no coordination overhead.

Because OneLake exposes the same ADLS Gen2 APIs and SDKs, any existing ADLS-compatible tool — Azure Data Factory, custom Python code using the Azure Storage SDK, or third-party connectors — connects to OneLake without modification [S2]. The ADLS compatibility layer is not an emulation; it is the same wire protocol.

### One Copy, Multiple Engines

The architectural payoff of one logical lake is that multiple Fabric engines can work against the same physical data without copying it [S2]. T-SQL in Fabric Data Warehouse, Apache Spark in Fabric Data Engineering, and the Analysis Services engine behind Power BI Direct Lake all read the same Delta-Parquet files. This eliminates the classic data-platform problem where the reporting copy is out of sync with the serving copy, and the serving copy is out of sync with the raw copy [S2].

### Resilience and Durability

For resilience, OneLake stores data on zone-redundant storage (ZRS) where the region supports it, and capacities can be created in paired Azure regions for disaster recovery purposes [S2]. Files deleted from OneLake are not immediately destroyed — OneLake soft delete retains them for seven days, and they can be recovered using Azure Storage Explorer or compatible tools [S2].

## Shortcuts: Connecting Data Without Moving It

### What a Shortcut Is

A OneLake shortcut is an object that points from a shortcut path within OneLake to a target path in a different storage location; reading through a shortcut retrieves data from the target without any physical copy being made [S4]. From the perspective of any Fabric engine reading through the OneLake API, a shortcut looks exactly like an ordinary folder — there is no special handling required in Spark, SQL, or KQL code [S4].

Shortcuts can be created in lakehouses and KQL databases, either interactively in the Fabric portal or programmatically through the Fabric REST API [S4]. They support a variety of target types: other locations within OneLake (lakehouses, warehouses, KQL databases, SQL databases), as well as external cloud stores including Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, Amazon S3, S3-compatible storage, and Google Cloud Storage [S1][S4].

### Internal vs. External Shortcuts

Internal OneLake shortcuts target data held in other Fabric items within the same tenant, with OneLake enforcing permissions by delegating to the identity of the calling user — no external credential is needed [S4]. External shortcuts (ADLS Gen2, S3, GCS) delegate authorization to a cloud connection that is bound at shortcut creation time; the connection is a privileged asset that must be managed separately from workspace membership [S4].

When external shortcuts are read through Power BI semantic models in DirectLake-over-SQL mode or via T-SQL in delegated scenarios, OneLake evaluates the caller's identity against the item permissions rather than using the bound cloud credential [S4]. This distinction matters for security design: the credential model differs depending on the engine making the request.

### Shortcut Caching and Performance

For cross-cloud external shortcuts, OneLake maintains a per-workspace file cache to reduce cross-cloud egress costs and latency [S4]. When shortcut targets are in a different cloud region, OneLake additionally applies intelligent caching to keep frequently used data close to the Fabric compute that accesses it [S1]. *Inference:* The cache is not a persistent replica — it is a read-through cache, and data in the cache does not affect durability guarantees on the source.

### Documented Shortcut Limits

A single Fabric item can hold up to 100,000 shortcuts, and a single OneLake path supports at most 10 levels of nested shortcut chaining [S4]. These are documented product limits, not soft defaults.

## Security Model

### Two Planes: Control and Data

OneLake security operates on two distinct planes [S3]. The control plane governs what users can do in the Fabric environment — creating items, sharing workspaces, triggering pipelines. The data plane governs what data a user can actually read or write within OneLake storage. A user can have workspace-level control plane access without necessarily having data-plane access to all the files in that workspace's items, and vice versa.

Authentication on the data plane is handled exclusively by Microsoft Entra ID for both users and service principals [S3]. There is no support for shared-access signatures (SAS tokens) or storage-account keys for OneLake data-plane access — every caller must present an Entra token.

### Hierarchical Permissions

Permissions in OneLake follow the storage hierarchy: workspace, item, and folder (specifically the Tables/ and Files/ top-level folders within a lakehouse) [S3]. Permissions set at the workspace level cascade downward to all items and their data. Item-level sharing permissions have specific scopes: Write grants both SQL and OneLake data access; ReadAll grants direct OneLake read access; Read grants SQL-only access through the SQL analytics endpoint, but not direct file access [S3].

Every lakehouse includes a built-in DefaultReader OneLake security role that grants any user holding the ReadAll item permission read access to the entire lakehouse namespace [S3]. Administrators can create custom OneLake security roles to restrict DefaultReader scope to specific tables or folders. A OneLake security role is composed of four parts: the data in scope, the permission granted, the members, and any row/column filter conditions [S3].

### Encryption and Transport

OneLake encrypts all data at rest by default using Microsoft-managed keys in a FIPS 140-2 compliant manner; key rotation is automatic [S3]. Inbound traffic to OneLake enforces at least TLS 1.2 and negotiates TLS 1.3 when supported; outbound Fabric compute connections to OneLake may use earlier versions in some configurations [S3].

### Tenant-Level Controls

Governance in OneLake is hierarchical: tenant-level security, compliance, and data-management policies automatically propagate to all workspaces and data items [S2]. A specific tenant admin setting controls whether applications running outside Fabric — for example, a custom ADLS API client or an external tool — can access OneLake data at all; when this setting is disabled, only Fabric-native engines can reach the data [S3].

OneLake audit log entries use ADLS-style operation names (CreateFile, DeleteFile, and so on), but the logs omit the client IP address — a limitation to account for in compliance architectures that require network-level attribution [S3].

Through the authorized engine model, external query engines can register with OneLake, pull security policy definitions, and apply them locally [S3]. This is the mechanism that allows Spark, T-SQL, and Analysis Services to enforce OneLake security roles without every row-level check round-tripping to a central policy service.

## Best Practices

**Let the single-copy model work for you.** The one-copy design is the core value proposition: load data once with Spark, query it with T-SQL, and serve it in Power BI Direct Lake — all from the same physical files [S2]. Resist the temptation to stage intermediate copies of the same data in different items; that recreates the silo problem OneLake is designed to eliminate.

**Use shortcuts to unify data without migration.** Rather than migrating all data into Fabric immediately, use OneLake shortcuts to bring existing ADLS Gen2, S3, or GCS storage into the namespace as read references [S1]. Pipelines and notebooks can operate on the shortcut path as if the data were native, while the source data remains in place.

**Scope security roles precisely.** The DefaultReader role grants read access to the entire lakehouse namespace, which is appropriate for many scenarios but too broad for fine-grained access control [S3]. Define custom OneLake security roles scoped to specific tables or folders for data that requires column-level or row-level restrictions.

**Use the Windows file explorer for ad-hoc access.** OneLake file explorer for Windows lets users browse all workspaces and data items and perform uploads, downloads, and edits through a familiar interface backed by the real OneLake storage [S2]. This is useful for operationally moving small files or verifying the state of a lakehouse without writing code.

## What Goes Wrong

**Siloed data lakes per business group.** Maintaining separate physical storage accounts or OneLake workspaces as isolated silos per team fragments governance and blocks cross-team analytics [S2]. The intent of OneLake is a single namespace — cross-workspace shortcuts are the correct mechanism for organizational boundaries, not separate lakes.

**Using workspace roles to enforce data-level restrictions.** OneLake security roles cannot restrict workspace Admins, Members, or Contributors — these workspace roles override any OneLake role definition applied to the same item [S3]. If a user is a workspace Member, no OneLake security role configuration will prevent them from reading data in that workspace. Data access restrictions must be enforced by keeping sensitive data in separate items with controlled sharing, not by security roles within a shared item.

**Spaces in shortcut table names.** The Delta Lake format does not permit spaces in table folder names. Creating a shortcut with a space in the name will cause failures in Delta-aware engines and is an antipattern to avoid [S4].

**Assuming shortcut deletion cascades.** Deleting a shortcut object removes the reference but does not delete the target data [S4]. Conversely, performing a delete operation *inside* a shortcut (deleting a file at the shortcut path) does write through to the target — the delete propagates to the actual storage location. These two operations have opposite behaviors and must not be confused.

## Performance and Internals

*This section covers L4 depth — implementation-level mechanics that are relevant for optimizing high-volume workloads.*

OneLake's virtual addressing model maps each workspace to an ADLS container and each item to a directory within that container [S2]. This means an ADLS-compatible tool that resolves paths will encounter a predictable, two-level namespace hierarchy below the tenant root.

External shortcut caching operates at the per-workspace level to reduce cross-cloud egress [S4]. Files read through an ADLS or S3 shortcut are stored in a workspace-local cache; subsequent reads of the same file version are served from cache without egressing to the origin cloud. The cache is read-through only — writes always bypass the cache and go directly to the target.

TLS 1.3 is negotiated for inbound OneLake connections where the client supports it, but outbound connections from some Fabric compute workloads may use TLS 1.2 [S3]. For compliance architectures with strict transport requirements, verify the specific Fabric compute surface in use rather than assuming tenant-wide TLS 1.3.

OneLake audit logs use familiar ADLS operation names but do not capture client IP addresses [S3]. For network-level audit requirements, supplement OneLake audit logs with Fabric workspace audit events and Entra ID sign-in logs, which do record client IP.

Through the authorized engine model, query engines pull and cache OneLake security policies locally [S3]. This enables row-level and column-level security to be enforced within the engine's execution plan rather than as a remote check, which keeps latency low for fine-grained access scenarios.

## Worked Example: Multi-Team Analytics Without Data Duplication

Consider a retailer with three teams: Supply Chain, Finance, and Marketing. Each team owns data in its own ADLS Gen2 storage account from a pre-Fabric era.

**Step 1 — Provision lakehouses.** Create a Fabric workspace per team. Each workspace automatically has a lakehouse backed by OneLake. *Inference:* One workspace per team is a reasonable governance boundary, though a single workspace with separate lakehouses per team also works.

**Step 2 — Create shortcuts to legacy storage.** In each lakehouse, create an ADLS Gen2 shortcut pointing to the team's existing storage container. The shortcut targets appear as folders named `Tables/supply_chain_inventory`, `Tables/finance_gl`, and `Tables/marketing_events` within their respective lakehouses. No data is copied [S4].

**Step 3 — Build a cross-team view.** In a shared Analytics workspace, create a new lakehouse. Add internal OneLake shortcuts from this lakehouse targeting the supply chain and finance Tables/ folders in the team lakehouses [S4]. A data engineer can now write a single Spark notebook or T-SQL query that joins supply chain inventory against finance general ledger, with OneLake enforcing the calling user's permissions on each shortcut target transparently [S4].

**Step 4 — Secure the shared lakehouse.** Grant the Analytics workspace only Read access for most analysts (SQL analytics endpoint only). For the two senior analysts who need direct file access, grant ReadAll. Do not rely on OneLake security roles to restrict workspace Contributors — if a user needs to be blocked from certain data, place that data in a separate item rather than sharing a workspace [S3].

**Step 5 — Confirm soft-delete coverage.** Verify that accidental deletion of shortcut paths is recoverable within the seven-day window by testing a restore with Azure Storage Explorer before going to production [S2].
